tagline: The story of Israel's kings from Solomon's glory and temple to a kingdom split in two, judged by one question: did the king walk with the LORD?
overview:
First Kings opens with David old and cold in his bed and a quarrel over who will succeed him. Solomon wins the throne, secures it with a series of executions, and asks God for wisdom to govern. His reign becomes Israel's golden age: wealth, international trade, famous wisdom, and above all the temple in Jerusalem, which Solomon builds and dedicates with a great prayer in chapter 8. Yet the same king gathers horses, gold, and hundreds of foreign wives, and in his old age his heart turns to other gods. After his death the kingdom tears in two. Ten northern tribes follow Jeroboam and form the kingdom of Israel, with its own shrines at Bethel and Dan, while the house of David keeps only Judah and Benjamin from Jerusalem.

The second half of the book follows the two kingdoms side by side, reign by reign, until it slows down for the ninth century BC and the dynasty of Omri. Ahab and his Phoenician queen Jezebel promote the worship of Baal, and God raises up the prophet Elijah to oppose them. The drought, the contest on Mount Carmel, Elijah's flight to Horeb, the murder of Naboth for his vineyard, and the prophet Micaiah standing alone against four hundred court prophets are among the most vivid scenes in the Old Testament. The book ends with Ahab dead in battle and his son Ahaziah on the throne, and the story runs straight on into 2 Kings.

First Kings matters because it asks what happens to a people when its leaders have every advantage and still turn from God. It shows the temple built and the promise to David kept, and in the same pages shows the seeds of the exile that 2 Kings will describe. Its heroes are not the kings but the prophets, who keep speaking God's word to power when power does not want to hear it.
author:
The book is anonymous. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud credits the books of Kings to the prophet Jeremiah, and there are real overlaps: 2 Kings 24:18-25:30 appears almost word for word as Jeremiah 52, and the two share language and concerns. Most modern scholars, however, see Kings as the work of one or more editors who shaped earlier sources into a single account. The book names some of those sources itself: the Book of the Acts of Solomon (1 Kings 11:41) and the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and of Judah, which it cites again and again as places where more could be read. These were probably royal annals or records drawn from them, and they are now lost.

Since the German scholar Martin Noth's work in the 1940s, many scholars have treated Deuteronomy through 2 Kings (without Ruth) as a single Deuteronomistic History, so called because it judges Israel's life by the standards of Deuteronomy: one place of worship, no other gods, and a king who obeys the law. Some think the history was compiled in stages, with a first edition in the time of King Josiah (late seventh century BC) and a final one during the exile; others think of a single exilic author. Conservative scholars often accept the use of sources and editorial shaping while stressing that the material is old and historically reliable. All agree that whoever wrote it had a prophetic outlook and a clear theological purpose.
date: First and 2 Kings were originally one book in the Hebrew Bible. The Greek translation called the Septuagint divided it and grouped it with Samuel as the four books of Kingdoms (or Reigns), and the division into two books later passed into Latin and English Bibles. The combined work in its final form can be no earlier than about 561 BC, because its last scene (2 Kings 25:27-30) describes the exiled King Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon in the thirty-seventh year of his exile. Nothing reports the return from exile under Cyrus in 539/538 BC, so most scholars date the finished book to the exile, roughly the middle of the sixth century BC. The sources behind it are much older, and the events of 1 Kings run from about 970 BC, when Solomon came to the throne, to about 850 BC.
setting:
The book is set in the tenth and ninth centuries BC. Solomon's reign (about 970 to 930 BC) came at a time when the great powers were weak: Egypt was divided and in decline, and Assyria had not yet begun its westward expansion. That window allowed a small kingdom in the hill country of Canaan to trade with Phoenician Tyre, whose king Hiram supplied cedar and craftsmen, to marry into Egypt's royal house, and to control trade routes. After the division of the kingdom around 930 BC, Pharaoh Shishak of Egypt (known from Egyptian records as Shoshenq I) raided Judah and took the temple treasures (1 Kings 14:25-26); he left a list of places he claimed to have conquered on a wall at Karnak.

In the ninth century the northern kingdom of Israel became a regional power under Omri and his son Ahab. Omri built a new capital at Samaria. The Moabite Stone (the Mesha Stele, found in 1868) names Omri as a king of Israel who oppressed Moab, and an Assyrian inscription of Shalmaneser III (the Kurkh Monolith) lists Ahab among the kings who fought Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC with a large force of chariots. Aram, the kingdom centered on Damascus, was Israel's frequent enemy. Ahab's marriage to Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, tied Israel to Phoenicia and brought the worship of Baal into the royal court. The first readers of the finished book, though, lived much later, in exile in Babylon after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, asking how their nation had come to this.
purpose: Kings is history written to explain and to call to repentance. Its first readers had lost the land, the temple, and the throne of David, and the book answers their question: why. The answer is not that the gods of Babylon were stronger, but that Israel and its kings broke covenant with the LORD, worshiped other gods, and ignored the prophets he sent. Each king is measured by whether he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and most fail. At the same time the book keeps hope alive. God keeps his promise to David even when the kings do not deserve it, preserving a lamp for David in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36; 15:4). Solomon's prayer in chapter 8 even anticipates exile and asks God to hear his people when they pray toward this place from a foreign land, which is exactly where the first readers found themselves.
story: First Kings follows directly from 2 Samuel. God promised David a son who would build a house for his name and a throne that would last forever (2 Samuel 7); in 1 Kings that son takes the throne and builds the temple. The book then traces how the united kingdom David built comes apart, and 2 Kings carries the two kingdoms to their ends: Israel to Assyria in 722 BC and Judah to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. First and 2 Chronicles later retell the same period from Judah's point of view for the community that returned from exile, and the prophets Elijah and Elisha, whose stories fill the end of 1 Kings and the start of 2 Kings, prepare the way for the writing prophets such as Amos and Hosea, who preached to the northern kingdom in the next century.
christ: First Kings keeps the promise to David alive through failure after failure, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David in whom that promise is finally kept (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32-33). Solomon, the wise son of David who builds God's house and brings peace, is a partial picture of a greater king, and Jesus draws the comparison himself: the Queen of the South came to hear Solomon's wisdom, and something greater than Solomon is here (Matthew 12:42). The temple, where God put his name and where sacrifices were offered and prayers heard, becomes a central image for Jesus, who spoke of his body as the temple (John 2:19-21). Elijah, too, points forward. Malachi promised that Elijah would come before the day of the LORD, and the Gospels identify John the Baptist as the one who came in Elijah's spirit and power (Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14), while Elijah himself appears with Moses beside Jesus at the transfiguration. These links are mostly patterns and promises rather than direct predictions, and the book's main contribution is to show why Israel needed a king who would not fail.
reading:
First Kings is theological history, written in narrative prose with lists, building records, speeches, and prayers set into it. Watch for the regnal formulas that open and close each reign (the king's age, the length of his reign, his mother's name for kings of Judah, a verdict on his faithfulness, and a reference to further records). These frame the story and tell you how the writer judges each ruler. Watch also for prophecy and fulfillment: again and again a prophet speaks, and later the narrator notes that it happened according to the word of the LORD.

A few misreadings are common. The book does not present Solomon's wealth as simple proof of God's approval; chapters 10 and 11 quietly show how his accumulation of gold, horses, and wives broke the rules for kings in Deuteronomy 17. The chronology of the kings is complex, because Israel and Judah counted reigns differently and sometimes had co-regencies, so the numbers can seem not to add up; scholars such as Edwin Thiele have proposed reconstructions, and several systems exist. And the Elijah stories are not only miracle tales: they are a contest over who is truly God in Israel.

structure.title: Solomon secures the throne
structure.summary: David's last days, Adonijah's bid for the crown, Solomon's anointing, David's charge, and the removal of Solomon's rivals.

structure.title: The wise king
structure.summary: Solomon asks for wisdom at Gibeon, judges between two mothers, and organizes a prosperous kingdom.

structure.title: The temple
structure.summary: Solomon gathers materials with Hiram of Tyre, builds the temple and his palace, makes its furnishings, and dedicates it with the ark, the cloud of glory, and a long prayer.

structure.title: Glory and decline
structure.summary: God's warning, Solomon's trade and fame, the visit of the Queen of Sheba, and then his foreign wives, idolatry, enemies, and death.

structure.title: The kingdom divided
structure.summary: Rehoboam's folly splits the kingdom; Jeroboam sets up golden calves; the reigns of both kingdoms are traced to the rise of Omri and Ahab.

structure.title: Elijah, Ahab, and the prophets
structure.summary: Elijah confronts Ahab and Baal worship, flees to Horeb, and calls Elisha; Ahab fights Aram, seizes Naboth's vineyard, and dies in battle as Micaiah foretold.

themes.title: The promise to David
themes.body: God swore to David that his house and kingdom would endure, and 1 Kings shows that promise holding through Solomon's accession, through the division of the kingdom, and through bad kings in Jerusalem. The reason Judah keeps a king of David's line is repeatedly said to be for David's sake. The promise is unconditional in its core and conditional in how each king experiences it, a tension the book leaves standing.

themes.title: One God, one place of worship
themes.body: Following Deuteronomy, the book judges kings by whether they worshiped the LORD alone and at the place he chose. Solomon's temple is the center of that vision. Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan, the high places, and Ahab's Baal worship are the great betrayals. Idolatry in Kings is never private; it shapes the whole nation's future.

themes.title: The word of the prophet
themes.body: Prophets such as Nathan, Ahijah, the man of God from Judah, Elijah, and Micaiah speak for God to kings. What they say comes true, and the narrator notes it. The book presents history as the working out of God's word, and it treats the prophet's lonely faithfulness as more important than royal power.

themes.title: Wisdom and its limits
themes.body: Solomon receives wisdom as a gift, and it makes him a just judge and a famous king. Yet the wisest man in Israel ends by following other gods. The book's sobering point is that wisdom without continued obedience does not protect a heart from drifting.

themes.title: Power and its abuse
themes.body: From forced labor on Solomon's buildings to Rehoboam's harsh answer and Ahab's theft of Naboth's vineyard, the book watches closely what kings do with power over ordinary people. God cares about a single vineyard owner, and he sends a prophet to say so.

keyChapters.why: Solomon asks for a discerning heart rather than riches or long life, and God gives him wisdom, shown at once in the judgment between two mothers.
The ark enters the temple, the glory fills it, and Solomon prays one of the Bible's great prayers, asking God to hear from heaven even when his people sin and are carried into exile.
Solomon's heart turns to other gods, and God announces that the kingdom will be torn from his son, leaving one tribe for David's sake.
Rehoboam's harsh answer divides the kingdom, and Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, the sin that shadows the northern kingdom to its end.
Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and fire from the LORD answers, a showdown over who is truly God.
The exhausted Elijah flees to Horeb, where God meets him not in wind, earthquake, or fire but in a quiet whisper, and sends him back to work.
Ahab and Jezebel murder Naboth to take his vineyard, and Elijah pronounces judgment, showing God's concern for justice to the powerless.
Micaiah alone tells Ahab the truth against four hundred prophets, and Ahab dies in battle just as the word of the LORD said.
